name: Risk Assessment Framework
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Weighing the Bet: A Framework for Sizing Up Technology Risk
lesson.summary: A risk assessment framework combines how likely an outcome is with how much it would matter if it happened, giving you a structured way to decide how seriously to take a technology claim instead of reacting to how loud or scary it sounds.
lesson.body:
Risk, in any serious engineering or financial sense, is the product of two separate numbers: how likely an outcome is, and how much it would matter if it happened. That multiplication step is easy to state and easy to skip. A common failure mode treats any nonzero chance of a catastrophic outcome as automatically requiring urgent action, no matter how small the probability, and an equally common opposite failure treats any claim with a low stated probability as safe to ignore entirely, no matter how severe the outcome would be if it happened. Both reactions skip the multiplication that a real risk assessment requires.

This is the same structure you already learned in the expected value framework, just pointed at threats instead of opportunities. Expected value asks you to sum, across possible outcomes, probability times payoff, in order to compare choices. Risk assessment applies the identical logic in the opposite direction: risk equals the probability of an adverse event times the magnitude of that adverse event. Both require honest, evidence grounded numbers rather than adjectives like huge or unlikely standing in for actual estimates, and both are only as good as the calibration work, base rate reasoning and due diligence, that goes into the numbers you plug in.

Apply this directly to a claim you will meet constantly in discussions of quantum computing: quantum computers will break current encryption. A responsible risk assessment separates the two variables. First, the probability that a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists within a given window of years: based on the base rate of technology roadmap slippage and the number of distinct hard breakthroughs still required, that probability is genuinely low in the near term, higher over twenty or thirty years, but still uncertain either way. Second, the impact if it does happen: severe, since it would compromise a large share of currently encrypted data and communications. A responsible assessment does not say low probability, so ignore it, and does not say severe impact, so panic, it multiplies the two together. It also has to account for a wrinkle that pure probability times impact can miss at first glance: some encrypted data has a very long shelf life, and an adversary can record it today and decrypt it later once the capability exists, an approach often called harvest now, decrypt later. That possibility raises the effective near term risk even while the capability itself remains distant, which is exactly why cryptographers are already migrating sensitive systems to post quantum algorithms, not because the threat is imminent, but because low probability multiplied by catastrophic, long lived impact still nets out to a real, worth managing risk, just not a start panicking today one.

The framework's real value is forcing you to keep the two variables separate so you can be honestly calibrated on each one independently, rather than letting a claim's emotional intensity, whether fear or excitement, substitute for that analysis. This is precisely the discipline you will lean on later in the course when writing a defensible executive brief: a good brief states likelihood and impact as two distinct, examined judgments, not as one blended feeling.
